summary: Describes Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation, a way to carry IPv4, IPv6, and other network packets directly over an MPEG-2 Transport Stream. It specifies a base format and an extension format for extra header information. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: ULE is a way to carry internet packets inside the television transport streams that digital TV uses. Each internet packet gets a short header and a checksum, and the result is fitted into the fixed-size television packets, several packets sharing one transport packet where there is room.

subtitle: Carries IP packets over the MPEG-2 transport streams used for digital television.

tldr.problem: Digital television uses MPEG-2 Transport Streams, which carry fixed 188-byte packets designed for video and audio. Running IP over the same network needs a way to put IP packets inside those, so a receiver can find them again.
tldr.mechanism: ULE wraps each IP packet in a small header and a CRC, then splits or packs the result into MPEG-2 transport packets. The header says how long the packet is and what kind it is, and optional extension headers can carry extra information.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from December 2005 and was later updated by RFC 7280. The header is deliberately small and simple to parse, which was the point of the design.

facts.label: Length field
facts.value: 15 bits, with the D bit in the top bit

today: RFC 4326 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005. It was later updated by RFC 7280; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Carrying IP over an MPEG-2 Transport Stream
sections.content:
This document describes an encapsulation for the transport of IP datagrams, or other network-layer packets, over ISO MPEG-2 Transport Streams. It satisfies the requirement for a lightweight encapsulation defined in RFC 4259: the basic header provides the required set of protocol fields, and extension headers may also be defined. This header structure is significantly simpler to parse and process than current alternative methods such as Multiprotocol Encapsulation, which builds upon the DSM-CC Table Section syntax.

The encapsulation is suited to services based on MPEG-2, for example the Digital Video Broadcast architecture, the Advanced Television Systems Committee system and other similar MPEG-2-based transmission systems. Such systems provide unidirectional physical and link-layer standards, and support has been defined for a wide range of physical media such as terrestrial, satellite and cable transmission. Bi-directional links may also be established using these standards, for example through the return channel technologies DVB defines or through dial-up modem links.

Protocol Data Units such as Ethernet frames, IP datagrams or other network-layer packets are passed to an Encapsulator. This formats each PDU into a SubNetwork Data Unit by adding an encapsulation header and an integrity check trailer. The SNDU is fragmented into a series of one or more MPEG-2 Transport Stream packets that are sent over a single TS Logical Channel. A format_identifier value has been registered for ULE with the hexadecimal value 0x554C4531, and Transport Streams that use the Programme Map Table and the ULE format SHOULD insert a descriptor with this value in the PMT ES_info descriptor loop. ULE Streams may also be identified by the stream_type value of 0x91 in a SI/PSI Table. This information may allow receivers and re-multiplexers to locate a specific ULE Stream, that is, the PID value of the TS Logical Channel that carries it.
sections.plainLanguage: Digital TV sends everything in fixed-size packets on a one-way link. ULE says how to slip an internet packet inside one of those, and how the receiver at the far end gets it back out.

sections.title: The MPEG-2 Machinery ULE Relies On
sections.content:
A TS Packet is a fixed-length 188-byte unit of data sent over a TS Multiplex. Each carries a 4-byte header plus optional overhead including an Adaptation Field, encryption details and time stamp information to synchronise related logical channels. The TS header fields used by this document are the Transport Error Indicator, the Payload Unit Start Indicator, the 13-bit Packet IDentifier that identifies the TS Logical Channel a packet belongs to, the Transport Scrambling Control, the 2-bit Adaptation Field Control and the 4-bit Continuity Counter.

When the PUSI bit is set to 1, one additional field follows the header: the Payload Pointer, an optional one-byte pointer containing the number of bytes that follow it, up to the start of the first Payload Unit. The PUSI bit also means the packet carries the start of a new Payload Unit, while a value of zero means it carries only the continuation or the end of one. The Adaptation Field may extend the TS Packet Header to carry timing and synchronisation information and may include stuffing bytes before the payload; Adaptation Field stuffing is not used in this encapsulation, and TS Packets from a ULE Encapsulator MUST be sent with an AFC value of '01', with receivers discarding TS Packets that carry other AFC values.

ULE uses private data, where the MPEG-2 standard leaves the meaning of the PUSI bit undefined, and follows the practice of PSI packets instead. A PUSI value of 0 means the TS Packet does not contain the start of an SNDU but contains the continuation or the end of one, while a value of 1 means the packet contains the start of an SNDU and a one-byte Payload Pointer follows the TS Packet header. All TS Packets comprising an SNDU MUST be assigned the same PID and therefore form part of the same TS Logical Channel. The all-ones PID value 0x1FFF indicates a Null TS Packet introduced to maintain a constant bit rate, and the all-zeros PID and other values are reserved for specific PSI/SI Tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Each television packet has a 4-byte header that says which channel it belongs to and whether it starts something new. ULE uses two of those header bits and one extra byte to mark where each encapsulated packet begins.

sections.title: The SNDU Format
sections.content:
PDUs are encapsulated using ULE to form an SNDU, and each SNDU is an MPEG-2 Payload Unit. The format is a D-bit, a Length field, a Type field, an optional Destination Address, the PDU itself, and a CRC-32 trailer. All multi-byte values in ULE are transmitted in network byte order.

The most significant bit of the Length field carries the Destination Address Absent field, the D-bit. A value of 0 indicates the presence of the Destination Address Field and a value of 1 indicates that it is not present. An End Indicator MUST be sent with a D-bit value of 1, and the default method SHOULD use a D-bit value of 0. The Length field is a 15-bit value giving the length in bytes of the SNDU from the byte following the Type field up to and including the CRC, and it includes the size of any extension headers that are present. When the first two bytes following an SNDU have the value 0xFFFF, this denotes an End Indicator, that is, an all-ones length combined with a D-bit value of 1, and it tells the receiver that there are no further SNDUs present within the current TS Packet.

The 16-bit Type field indicates the type of payload carried in an SNDU, or the presence of a Next-Header. The values are divided in two, similar to the allocations for Ethernet: the first set, the values less than 1536 decimal, are IANA assigned and indicate the Next-Header, while the second set, the values 1536 and above, are identical to the corresponding type codes specified for Ethernet and recorded in the IANA EtherType registry. The document defines 0x0000 for a Test SNDU, 0x0001 for a Bridged Frame and 0x0100 for Extension-Padding in the first space, and gives 0x0800 for IPv4 payload and 0x86DD for IPv6 payload as examples of the second.

The SNDU Destination Address Field is optional. It MUST be carried for IP unicast packets destined to routers that are sent using shared links, where the same link connects multiple receivers. When present, a Network Point of Attachment field directly follows the fourth byte of the SNDU header. NPA destination addresses are 6-byte numbers used to identify the receivers in an MPEG-2 transmission network that should process a received SNDU. The value 0x00:00:00:00:00:00 MUST NOT be used, the least significant bit of the first byte is set to 1 for multicast frames, and 0xFF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF is the link broadcast address. When the PDU is an IP multicast packet and a destination address is present, the IP group address MUST be mapped to the multicast SNDU destination address using the method used to generate a destination MAC address in Ethernet.

Each SNDU MUST carry a 32-bit CRC field in the last four bytes. The CRC-32 polynomial is used, the same one as in Ethernet, with the generator polynomial 0x104C11DB7. The Encapsulator initialises the accumulator to 0xFFFFFFFF, accumulates all bytes from the start of the SNDU header to the end of the SNDU excluding the trailer, and places the result in the CRC field. The receiver recomputes the value and discards SNDUs that do not have a valid CRC, entering the Idle State.
sections.plainLanguage: Each wrapped packet carries its length, its kind, an optional address for the receiver meant to take it, and a checksum at the end. The receiver checks the checksum and throws away anything that does not add up.

sections.title: Extension Headers
sections.content:
In ULE, a Type field value less than 1536 decimal indicates an Extension Header, and these values are assigned from a separate IANA registry. The use of a single Type and Next-Header field simplifies processing and eliminates the need to maintain multiple registries. The cost is that each Extension Header requires at least 2 bytes, justified on the basis of simplified processing and a simple lightweight header for the common case when no extensions are present.

A ULE Extension Header is identified by a 16-bit value in the Type field, organised as a 5-bit zero prefix, a 3-bit H-LEN field and an 8-bit H-Type field. An H-LEN value of 0 indicates a Mandatory Extension Header, which has a pre-defined length that is not communicated in the field, and no additional limit is placed on its maximum length. A Mandatory Extension Header MAY modify the format or encoding of the enclosed PDU, for example to perform encryption or compression. H-LEN values from 1 to 5 indicate Optional Extension Headers of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 bytes in total including the 2-byte Type field, and the H-LEN value indicates the total number of bytes in an Optional Extension Header. Values of 6 or more indicate that the combined H-LEN and H-TYPE values give the EtherType of the PDU that directly follows the Type field. The H-Type is a one-byte field that is either one of 256 Mandatory Header Extensions or one of 256 Optional Header Extensions.

Several Extension Headers may be chained in series, with each Type below 1536 indicating another extension and the final Type above 1535 giving the EtherType of the payload. Two examples are defined here. The Test SNDU is a Mandatory Extension Header of Type 1 that must be the final or only extension header in the chain; the structure of its data is not defined, and receivers MAY record reception in a log file but MUST then discard any Test SNDUs. The Extension-Padding Optional Extension Header results in any following option header being ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Some packets need extra information, such as a bridging header or a place to note that encryption has been applied. ULE lets a sender insert extra small headers before the payload, and each one says how long it is.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Padding and Packing
sections.content:
When an Encapsulator has not previously sent a TS Packet for a specific TS Logical Channel, or after an idle period, it starts to send an SNDU in the first available TS Packet. This first TS Packet generated MUST carry a PUSI value of 1 and a Payload Pointer value of zero, indicating that the SNDU starts immediately after the Payload Pointer in the payload. The encapsulation MUST ensure that all TS Packets set the MPEG-2 Continuity Counter carried in the TS Packet header, and this value MUST be incremented by one, modulo 16, for each successive TS Packet containing a fragment or complete SNDU sent using the same TS Logical Channel.

An Encapsulator MAY decide not to send another SNDU immediately even if space is available in a partially filled TS Packet. This procedure is known as Padding. The End Indicator informs the receiver that there are no more SNDUs in this TS Packet payload, and it is followed by zero or more unused bytes until the end of the payload, all of which MUST be set to the value 0xFF. The Padding procedure trades decreased efficiency against improved latency.

Alternatively, when more packets are waiting at the Encapsulator and a TS Packet has sufficient space remaining in the payload, the Encapsulator can follow a previously encapsulated SNDU with another SNDU using the next available byte of the payload. This is called Packing, and it is what allows a single TS Packet to carry more than one SNDU, or part of one. The size and number of SNDUs SHOULD be adjusted so that the resulting RTP packet is not larger than the path MTU; to handle larger packets, the format relies on lower layers for fragmentation, which may result in reduced performance.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender has two choices when a transport packet has room left. It can stop and fill the rest with a marker, or it can squeeze another internet packet in after the first. Packing saves bandwidth; padding gets data out sooner.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for ULE resemble those that arise when the existing Multiprotocol Encapsulation is used, and ULE does not add specific new threats that will impact the security of the general Internet. There is a known security issue with uninitialised stuffing bytes, and in ULE these bytes are set to 0xFF as normal practice in MPEG-2. There are known integrity issues with the removal of the LAN FCS in a bridged networking environment, which exposes the traffic to potentially undetected corruption while being processed by the Encapsulator or the receiver.

There is a potential security issue when a receiver receives a PDU with two Length fields, since the receiver would need to validate the actual length and the Length field and ensure that inconsistent values are not propagated by the network. In direct encapsulation of IPv4 and IPv6 in ULE this is avoided by including only one SNDU Length Field, but the issue still arises in bridged LLC frames, and frames with an LLC Length greater than the SNDU payload size MUST be discarded, with an SNDU payload length error SHOULD be recorded.

In the future a ULE Mandatory Extension Header may be used to define a method to perform link encryption of the SNDU payload, as an additional security mechanism to IP, transport or application layer security and not a replacement for it. The method of encryption and the way in which keys are exchanged is beyond the scope of the specification, as are the definition of the security association format and of the related encryption keys.
sections.plainLanguage: ULE does not add new threats of its own, but it inherits the old ones. Bridged frames lose their link-layer checksum on the way, and a future extension header is the intended place to add encryption if it is ever needed.

sections.title: The Next-Header Registry
sections.content:
IANA has created the ULE Next-Header Type field registry, which allocates Next-Header values within the range 0 to 511. For each allocated value it also specifies the set of allowed H-LEN values, and in combination these define the allowed values in the range 0 to 1535 for the first part of the ULE Type space. The registry must not allocate values greater than 0x01FF.

The registry is subdivided in two. Values 0 to 255 are IANA-assigned values indicating Mandatory Extension Headers, or link-dependent Type fields, for ULE, requiring expert review leading to prior issue of an IETF RFC. The specification must define the value and the name associated with the Extension Header together with the procedure for processing it, must define the need for the Mandatory Extension and its intended use, and must specify the size of the Extension Header. Two assignments have been made in this document: Type 0 is the Test-SNDU and Type 1 is the Bridged-SNDU.

Values 256 to 511 are IANA-assigned values indicating Optional Extension Headers for ULE, again requiring expert review leading to prior issue of an IETF RFC. The entry must specify the range of allowable H-LEN values that are permitted, in the range 1 to 5, and must define the need for the Optional Extension and its intended use. One assignment has been made in this document: Type 256 is Extension-Padding, with H-LEN values 1 to 5.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps one list for the extra headers. The bottom half means the header is compulsory and has a fixed length; the top half means it is optional and says its own length. Only two entries exist today, and they are only for testing.

viz.caption: THE SNDU HEADER, WITH THE PDU BETWEEN THE ADDRESS AND THE CHECKSUM

fields.name: D and Length
fields.desc: The top bit says whether a destination address follows. The other 15 bits give the length up to and including the CRC.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Below 1536 it points at an extension header; 1536 and above it is the EtherType of the payload.

fields.name: Destination Address
fields.desc: Optional 6-byte network point of attachment address. The broadcast address is all ones.

fields.name: CRC-32
fields.desc: Integrity check over the header and payload, using the polynomial 0x104C11DB7.

items.label: Extension-Padding
items.desc: An optional extension header that makes the following header be ignored.

items.label: IPv4 payload
items.desc: The payload is a complete IPv4 datagram.

items.desc: The payload is a complete IPv6 datagram.
